volumes.heading: Volume I · History and Business
volumes.thesis: How Minecraft grew from a 2009 prototype into a medium that communities, platforms, and capital kept redeveloping. Four parts: origins, becoming a culture, life after the acquisition, and a dissection of the business model. Not a changelog — a study of how choices grew into structure.

parts.title: Origins (2009–2011)
parts.intent: How a working prototype grew into a product on open development and a minimal loop.

chapters.title: From Infiniminer to Cave Game
chapters.desc: Infiniminer was abandoned and open-sourced less than a month after release; its "clone" became the best-selling game of all time. This chapter digs into the prehistory of destructible space — what Cave Game threw away, and how "unfinished" let it live as a product.

chapters.title: Alpha: Developing in Public
chapters.desc: From Survival Test to Infdev, the world went from finite to infinite. The paid Alpha turned players into co-authors through weekly updates — and turned trust into a promise that had to be repaid continuously.

chapters.title: Mojang, Beta, and the Release Version
chapters.desc: When a personal project becomes a studio, design authority moves from intuition to organization. Beta 1.8 was the first convergence toward a game; 1.0 completed a ceremony, not a system; and buy-once pricing set the ground note of every later revenue conflict.

parts.title: Becoming a Culture (2011–2014)
parts.intent: How authors outside the base game defined in reverse what Minecraft is.

chapters.title: Mods as the Second Author
chapters.desc: Mods grew up alongside the game itself — Forge took the client seat, Bukkit the server, resource packs the skin. This chapter traces how the second authorship formed, and why Mojang absorbed the piston but left industry outside.

chapters.title: The Server Is the New Game
chapters.desc: Players buy the client but play a different game living on a server. Creative, survival, and minigame servers are three societies on one engine; Hypixel and 2b2t are its two extremes — and the infrastructure beneath it all is more fragile than the game itself.

chapters.desc: Let's Plays, tutorials, animations, and parody songs wrote Minecraft into the shared language of children and families, and Education Edition carried it into classrooms. Once "how to play" lives in video, what the base game should still teach becomes a late design question.

parts.title: After the Acquisition (2014–)
parts.intent: How capital, two product lines, and version politics turned protection into governance.

chapters.title: The Microsoft Acquisition
chapters.desc: What $2.5 billion bought was not "can we still add blocks" but distribution, accounts, compliance, and cross-platform reach. This chapter checks the community's fears from 2014 against what actually happened, item by item, to see what the deal really bought.

chapters.desc: From Pocket Edition to Bedrock, cross-platform was the product logic; feature divergence is brand debt. The Marketplace commercialized player creations and shut modding culture outside the gate. Two Minecrafts, not two skins.

chapters.desc: From Notch tossing things in to themed versions: snapshots, experimental toggles, and datapacks turned the development process itself into an interface the community co-writes — while vanilla purity and the mob vote expose the real fight over who gets to define Minecraft.

parts.title: Dissecting the Business Model
parts.intent: Revenue, grey economy, competition, and legacy on one map.

chapters.title: The Revenue Structure
chapters.desc: The one-time purchase is only the first layer. This chapter takes Minecraft's money apart into three layers — client and subscriptions, IP licensing, access and regional publishing — then asks the reverse question: where the money cannot come from, and why "a cut of mods" never stood on Java Edition.

chapters.title: The Grey Economy
chapters.desc: Free mods sell the paid game, and the biggest server networks take millions a year without paying Mojang a cent. This chapter explains why Minecraft's community creation is at once gaming's most open ecosystem and the one platforms find hardest to take a cut from.

chapters.title: Minecraft as Cultural Heritage
chapters.desc: Versions, saves, servers, and mods are all harder to preserve than the engine. Java has the launcher as a backstop; Bedrock has almost no way back. Brand safety and creative freedom have begun to chafe — who preserves a world people actually live in?

volumes.payoffFan: See how a handful of rules combinatorially explode over a voxel world — the spine of the book.
volumes.payoffDev: Transferable principles with their premises spelled out; Volume II is the frozen layer everything else cites.
volumes.heading: Volume II · Game Design
volumes.thesis: Depth comes not from content volume but from the combinatorial explosion of a very few rules over a voxel world. Four parts: design primitives, how systems interlock, social design, and transferable principles. The book's spine is this volume.

parts.title: Design Primitives
parts.intent: The voxel, verbs, survival, and Creative mode — the frozen layer.

chapters.title: The Voxel as a Design Primitive
chapters.desc: The one-meter cube serves building, walking, fighting, and redstone at once because space is discrete, breakable, placeable, and countable. The world is the inventory; the voxel is not an art style — it is a system of measurement.

chapters.title: The Minimal Verb Set and Game Feel
chapters.desc: Look, walk, dig, place, craft, attack, use — seven verbs carry a whole game. This chapter explains why shipping without a build mode or a skill tree was the right call, and how tools amplify verbs instead of adding keys.

chapters.title: Survival as a Meaning Machine
chapters.desc: Hunger, night, and death are not a difficulty curve but rhythm devices: they hand out no goals, only moments that demand a response. The wood-stone-iron-diamond ladder is false progress, real teaching; home and safety are self-built; death drops, but does not destroy.

chapters.title: Creative Mode Is Not a Level Editor
chapters.desc: Survival, Creative, Adventure, and Spectator are four permission configurations on one physics, not four games. Creative is parasitic on Survival's blocks, scale, and physics; infinite resources change the builder's social identity, not the world's rules.

parts.title: How Systems Interlock
parts.intent: How crafting, worldgen, redstone, commands, mobs, and dimensions interlock.

chapters.title: Crafting, Items, and Inventory
chapters.desc: Depth is not added to the character but to things: grid crafting makes recipe knowledge a community dialect, items are portable slices of the world, and durability and enchanting build growth into objects. Anti-RPG was a choice, not an absence.

chapters.desc: The electricity metaphor failed, yet logic circuits grew out of the wreckage. The game teaches nothing, so the community wrote the textbook; gates, clocks, flying machines, and computers are computation invented by players. This chapter erects the "misusable system": designers deliver physics, not a play list.

parts.intent: Multiplayer defaults, who makes rules, mods as design method.

chapters.desc: Singleplayer worlds are full of design prepared for others — doors, beds, chests, signs. LAN, Realms, and public servers are three social radii; seeds, mods, and video reconnect a singleplayer save to society, with delay. Multiplayer is the default state, not an add-on mode.

chapters.desc: The one-meter grid, the breakable world, the minimal verb set, outsourced goals, misusable physics, a world that outlives the engine, redevelopment as a first-class citizen — seven invariants examined one by one, each with its degradation scenario and its criterion for being falsified.

chapters.title: Discardable Accidents
chapters.desc: The Java runtime, the one global 20-TPS clock, the dual-edition split, the semantic freeze on parts of the implementation — every one of these accidents can be discarded, but each must first prove that the invariant it hosted has somewhere new to live.

parts.title: Architecture Proposal
parts.intent: World representation, scheduling, scripting, network, rendering.

chapters.title: World Representation
chapters.desc: Sparse voxels, componentized state, the world as an object, deterministic replay, old saves as first-class citizens — the rewritten world representation must serve, at once, one big world housing tens of thousands and tens of thousands of small worlds each their own.

chapters.title: Simulation Scheduling
chapters.desc: Interest as a first-class citizen, causality-tiered settlement, explicit entity budgets, reproducible time travel — a scheduling design in which singleplayer and ten-thousand-player servers share one kernel, and how redstone causality keeps from being torn apart.

chapters.title: The Two Layers of Scripts and Mods
chapters.desc: The sandbox layer and the native layer each fail alone — two single-layer designs and the exact ways they die, the separation of blast radii, three lines of stable API, hot reload and versioned schemas, and author experience as a formal part of the product.

chapters.title: Networking, Permissions, and the Sinking of Social Functions
chapters.desc: Land claims, backups, rollbacks, replay arbitration, permission tiers — the "standard legal code" every server owner legislates over and over should sink into the engine as first-class functions; ownership becomes a first-class concept, anticheat becomes system structure, and the four modes generalize into a continuous permission matrix.

chapters.title: Rendering and Authoring Tools
chapters.desc: The hand-feel is still the product, and rendering debt should be cleared natively along directions the community has already validated; structure editing, function debugging, and data inspection should be built in as the author seat's basic infrastructure — and tools and runtime must share one world model.

chapters.title: The Compatibility Strategy
chapters.desc: Old saves and the old ecosystem are the rewrite's ticket of admission: this chapter argues why reading old saves is an obligation rather than a feature, lays out three channels for reading them and the two-path plan for redstone, and shows how namespace discipline and the costs of compatibility get written into the product's scope.

chapters.title: Who Holds the Right to Rewrite
chapters.desc: Protocol, assets, and brand are habitually conflated. This chapter takes the three apart, inventories what community projects, the officials, and open source can each promise — and are fated never to promise — and swaps the acceptance standard from "more alike" back to "the invariants still hold."

chapters.desc: The book's closing word: the finalized list of essential properties, the three verb claims collected and one amendment confessed; and an answer to the most important question — if no one ever rewrites, why this volume was still worth writing.
